newsitem.title: USA: Embattled Tarses says she will stay at ABC.
newsitem.headline: Embattled Tarses says she will stay at ABC.

text.p: ABC Entertainment President Jamie Tarses Wednesday insisted she has no plans to leave the network, putting to rest rumours she was going to step down or be fired after only a year on the job.
At a news conference for television writers previewing ABC's fall lineup, Tarses, 33, said she was committed to the network and "very, very excited" about working to improve ABC's ratings.
"It's what gets me out of bed every morning -- the prospect of ultimately getting our network back to No. 1," she said to a room packed with television journalists.

Her tenure at the No. 3 network has made headlines in New York and Hollywood in recent weeks since ABC hired veteran TV executive Stuart Bloomberg as chairman of the Entertainment division over Tarses. The shakeup was widely viewed as a sign the company's top brass had lost confidence in her ability, a controversy that intensified last week when Tarses was featured in The New York Times Magazine criticising her bosses and strongly suggesting she may leave the network.

Asked about that story on Wednesday, a nervous Tarses said she had taken a "brief moment" to consider her plans after learning of Bloomberg's appointment but had decided that working as a team "could really be quite wonderful." She refused to elaborate on the New York Times article.

Tarses became the first woman ever to head a network's entertaiment division when ABC hired her a little over a year ago from NBC. At NBC she had been highly regarded for helping develop such top-rated programmes as "Friends" and "Mad About You", but since joining the rival network the attention she has received has been more about her personal struggles as a woman in the top levels of management.

Those issues were again highlighted Wednesday when reporters invited to ask Tarses and Bloomberg about programming and scheduling decisions turned instead to the drama in the executive offices and sexism in the industry.

As the questioning became more and more personal, Tarses was asked about her judgment shortly after joining ABC in giving a lucrative contract to her boyfriend Robert Morton, and whether the recent controversy had made her feel like the most hated woman in Hollywood.

"I've always looked at it as an individual doing the job, not as a man or a woman and I will continue to do so," said Tarses, whose voice sometimes cracked under the intense questioning. Bloomberg, seated next to her, also tried to elevate the tone of the news conference, remarking, "I'm not really good at this spin thing. So what I'll say is we're sitting here together happily. I've been in the job three weeks and it's been really great. We're having a great time."
ABC President Robert Iger showed up at the news conference to lend support to Tarses and Bloomberg.

Asked if having two executives making decisions about programming would present problems, Iger said: "I think it's a complicated enough job that to have more people figuring it out is better than having fewer people."
The news conference capped a three-day press tour at which ABC outlined its strategy to win viewers back from NBC and stem the loss of audiences to cable.

To that end, ABC will air what it considers its best new programmes on Thursday night, against NBC's top-rated "Seinfeld" and "Friends". Rather than trying to compete with similar hip, urban comedies, ABC is betting on the success of two new hour-long dramas, "Nothing Sacred", about an inner-city priest facing challenges to his faith, and "Cracker", about an offbeat psychologist who helps police solve difficult cases.

Another cornerstone of ABC's strategy is to revamp Saturday night with three hour-long dramas: "C-16:FBI", about a group of federal agents in Los Angeles, "Total Security", about a private investigating firm, and "The Practice", a critically acclaimed show that first aired last year about a Boston law firm more interested in doing good than in making money.
